title: Processing: Getting "In" to Empty
coreMove: Process each captured item to empty by deciding what it is, whether it is actionable, what outcome or next action it requires, and where its reminder belongs.

exampleSpecs.domain: a charge nurse sorting the paper tray after a double-booked clinic morning
exampleSpecs.audience: a hospital nurse responsible for patient follow-up
exampleSpecs.stakes: a lab callback, a supply request, or a patient instruction could disappear into the same pile and create real risk
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the nurse processes one item at a time and refuses to put anything back undecided, routing each paper to trash, reference, calendar, waiting-for, or a next-action list

exampleSpecs.domain: a family court attorney opening twelve voicemails before a filing deadline
exampleSpecs.audience: a lawyer with client calls, court dates, and delegated paralegal work converging at once
exampleSpecs.stakes: a client affidavit could be late because the attorney confuses listening to messages with deciding what each one means
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the attorney states the desired outcome and next physical action for each actionable message, then parks delegated pieces on a waiting-for list instead of trusting memory

exampleSpecs.domain: a sous-chef reviewing the prep clipboard after a chaotic lunch rush
exampleSpecs.audience: a restaurant kitchen lead preparing for dinner service
exampleSpecs.stakes: service could stall if vague notes like 'fix station' remain as complaints rather than defined actions
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the example shows vague kitchen notes becoming either discarded noise, reference, a project outcome, or a visible next action such as 'ask produce vendor about missing basil before 3 p.m.'

exampleSpecs.domain: a parent emptying second-grade backpacks and the kitchen mail counter on Sunday evening
exampleSpecs.audience: a household captain managing school forms, bills, invitations, and small errands
exampleSpecs.stakes: a permission slip, a bill, and a birthday response can keep nagging all week if they stay in a mixed pile
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the parent uses the two-minute rule only for truly quick completions and otherwise sends each item to calendar, next action, someday-maybe, reference, or trash until the counter is empty

exampleSpecs.domain: a museum registrar returning from a donor meeting with notes, business cards, and photo requests
exampleSpecs.audience: a cultural-institution administrator who handles commitments across donors, curators, and shipping staff
exampleSpecs.stakes: a loan agreement can become ambiguous if meeting notes are treated as processed merely because they were rewritten neatly
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the postmortem identifies the failure as a processed-looking pile with no decisions, then repairs it by assigning every note to reference, action, calendar, or waiting-for

exampleSpecs.domain: a freelance cellist between rehearsals with texts about gigs, sheet music, travel, and an instrument repair receipt
exampleSpecs.audience: an independent musician juggling commitments without an office staff
exampleSpecs.stakes: a double booking or missing score could happen if messages are repeatedly reread but not clarified
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the reveal shows that relief comes not from rereading or answering everything, but from putting hard dates on the calendar and physical next actions on the right lists

exampleSpecs.domain: a shelter coordinator processing donation offers after a storm
exampleSpecs.audience: a nonprofit operations coordinator facing urgent community messages
exampleSpecs.stakes: needed supplies could be delayed while the inbox fills with duplicates, unsuitable offers, and half-commitments
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the coordinator resists treating every urgent-looking message as equal and routes each one as trash, reference, delegated pickup, waiting-for, calendar, or a deferred next action
